blocks.content: Arunachal Pradesh has a predominantly natural resource-based economy with agriculture, horticulture, hydropower, and forestry as its main pillars. Despite its vast natural wealth, the state faces challenges of geographical isolation, poor infrastructure, and sparse population density.
4.1 Overview of State Economy

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Agriculture and horticulture serve as the primary economic drivers in Arunachal Pradesh.
Traditional Jhum cultivation (shifting agriculture) is widely practiced along with terrace farming.
The Ziro Valley is globally renowned for the sustainable Apatani wet rice-cum-fish farming system.
Arunachal Pradesh holds vast untapped hydropower resources, positioning it as the potential Power Capital of India.
Forest resources contribute significantly to the state economy through bio-resources and timber.
Transport and connectivity are expanding through strategic road, air, and railway infrastructure projects.

cells: Among smaller GSDP states due to small population

blocks.content: 4.2 Agriculture and Horticulture

Agriculture is the backbone of Arunachal Pradesh's rural economy. Jhum (shifting) cultivation has been practiced for millennia, though settled agriculture is increasingly being promoted. The state has significant horticulture potential due to its varied climate.
Jhum Cultivation (Shifting Agriculture)

Jhum cultivation involves clearing a patch of forest, burning the vegetation, cultivating it for 1–2 seasons, and then moving to a new area while the earlier plot is left fallow for 8–15 years. Though ecologically controversial, it is deeply integrated into the cultural practices of many tribes.
Important Crops

cells: Oranges, kiwi fruit, passion fruit, pineapple, banana

blocks.content: Ziro Valley — Apatani Farming System
Hydropower — The Power Capital of India

The Ziro Valley in Lower Subansiri district is famous for the Apatani tribe's unique paddy-cum-fish farming system. The Apatanis practice wet rice cultivation integrated with fish rearing in the paddy fields — a practice that achieves high productivity without using any agrochemicals. This system has been recognised by UNESCO and is a candidate for World Heritage status.
4.3 Hydropower — The Power Capital of India

Arunachal Pradesh has been called the 'Powerhouse of India' or the 'Future Power Capital of India' due to its enormous hydropower potential. The state has an assessed hydropower potential of approximately 50,328 MW — the highest of any Indian state.

The Subansiri Lower HEP has been one of the most controversial hydropower projects in the country due to environmental concerns and protests from downstream communities in Assam. The Dibang Multipurpose Project, if completed, will be one of the tallest dams in the world.
4.4 Forests and Forest Economy

rows: Slash-and-burn shifting agriculture on hill slopes
Integrated wet rice cultivation with fish farming (paddy-cum-fish culture)

blocks.content: Forests cover over 80% of Arunachal Pradesh's area, making it one of the most forested states in India. The state has four broad types of forests: tropical evergreen, subtropical, temperate, and alpine.

items: State Forest Department regulates timber, bamboo, and non-timber forest produce (NTFP).
Major NTFP include cane, bamboo, medicinal plants, honey, mushrooms, and lac.
The Forest Rights Act (2006) has significantly impacted forest governance by recognising tribal rights.
Eco-tourism is being developed as an alternative to commercial forest exploitation.

blocks.content: 4.5 Industries
Large-scale industry is largely absent in Arunachal Pradesh. The industrial landscape is dominated by small and cottage industries:

items: Handloom and handicraft industries — a major source of livelihood for tribal women
Agro-based industries — ginger processing, orange juice, and spice processing
Bamboo industries — furniture, handicrafts, construction materials
Eco-tourism and adventure tourism — river rafting, trekking, bird watching
NERAMAC (North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation) assists in marketing NE produce
Pharmaceutical industries — small scale, at Pasighat and Naharlagun

blocks.content: 4.6 Transport and Connectivity
Connectivity has been one of the biggest challenges for Arunachal Pradesh. The state has seen significant improvement in recent decades, particularly in road and air connectivity.
Roads

items: Apatani Farming System: Frequently tested regarding eco-friendly integrated wet rice and fish cultivation in Ziro Valley.
Jhum Cultivation: Questions often cover shifting agriculture practices and ecological impact in North-East India.
Strategic Infrastructure: Key exam focus on Arunachal Pradesh's major hydropower projects and transport corridors (Road, Rail, Air).

blocks.content: The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) plays a vital role in constructing and maintaining strategic roads. The Trans-Arunachal Highway (TAH), currently under construction, will connect Tawang in the west to Kanubari in the east, passing through the state capital Itanagar.
Air Connectivity
Railways

Arunachal Pradesh is the last major state to be connected by railway. The first train service reached Naharlagun (near Itanagar) in 2014. Extension of railways to Itanagar and beyond is under progress. The Harmuti–Naharlagun rail link was the first in the state.
